newsitem.title: ITALY: Court ruling could shake up Italian law making.
newsitem.headline: Court ruling could shake up Italian law making.

text.p: Italy's Constitutional Court was reported on Tuesday to have banned a key legislative practice in a move that could force the government and parliament into a radical rethink of how they make laws

Corriere della Sera newspaper said the court had ruled unconstitutional the practice by which governments have extended laws drawn up by cabinet decree, an instrument originally intended only to be applied in extraordinary circumstances.
Decrees have validity for 60 days, after which they lapse unless parliament has converted them into law.
Given the snail's pace passage of legislation through parliament, successive cabinets have frequently reissued decrees when they are about to expire.
Tuesday's report said the court's ruling, which has yet to be published, would ban the re-issue of decrees.
A spokesman for the court would neither confirm nor deny the report but Enrico Micheli, a senior aide to Prime Minister Romano Prodi, said the ruling would cause severe problems.
He said the centre-left government, appointed in May, had inherited a backlog of about 100 repeat decrees awaiting passage, which it had since scaled down to 50.
"Among these 50 outstanding decrees some are very important. The problem is to find a way of getting them passed into law in the shortest possible time," he told Italian radio.

Corriere said outstanding decrees included bills relating to part of the 1996 budget, early retirement measures for staff at Alitalia that are part of the airline's restructuring plans and funds earmarked for building projects for Rome's 2000 Jubilee.
Micheli said he expected the ruling to become effective upon publication and that it would not be retroactive.

Livio Paladin, a former constitutional court chairman, said the ruling would compel President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro to honour a threat he made at the opening of parliament in May not to sign any re-issued decrees.

"Decrees have become a boomerang in so far as the government is no longer capable of getting a new decree or ordinary law through parliament because parliament is so bogged down in examining (outstanding) decrees," Paladin said.
Corriere said the ruling was so sensitive that the court had so far advised only Scalfaro, Prodi and the speakers of the two houses of parliament.
It published the story amid fresh political squabbling over whether to establish a new bicameral parliamentary commission to propose reforms to the way Italy is governed.
Part of its job would be to suggest ways to streamline the cumbersome workings of Italy's two houses of parliament.

The Chamber of Deputies and the Senate must approve precisely the same text of any law for it to take effect. Any item of legislation, including decrees, must be examined in various commissions before going before the full assemblies.

Political sources said the court ruling could encourage a deal between Prodi's "Olive Tree" bloc and the centre-right opposition to set up the commission. A law establishing it has already been passed but requires a second reading in parliament.
